Introduction to Statics and Vectors

Statics
ENGI 10130 problems
We’ll work through these together in class.
Problem 1
Ch. 1 — Weight from Mass (W = mg)
A crate of mass $m = 75\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs at rest from a single vertical cable attached to a ceiling hook at $A$. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Determine the tension $T$ in the cable.
Crate hanging from a vertical cable
Determine the cable tension $T$.
Solution
736 N
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of the crate
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the crate by cutting the cable. Two forces act on it: the cable tension $T$ pulling upward at the top of the crate, and the weight $W$ acting downward through the center $G$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $m = 75\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $T$.
Step 3State the model: The crate is at rest, so it is in equilibrium. The cable is vertical and its own weight is neglected.
Step 4Set axes and sign convention: $+y$ upward, $+x$ to the right.
Step 5Write the weight law: $W = mg$. This is Newton's second law $F = ma$ with $a = g$; it converts a mass in kg into a force in N.
Step 6Substitute numbers: $$W = (75\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2})$$
Step 7Compute the weight: $W = 735.75\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2} = 735.75\ \mathrm{N}$, since $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$.
Step 8Sum forces in x: $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically because no force has a horizontal component.
Step 9Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ T - W = 0$. Both forces share one vertical line of action through $G$, so $\sum M_G = 0$ is also satisfied automatically.
Step 10Rearrange: $T = W$.
Step 11State the result: $T = 735.75\ \mathrm{N} \approx 736\ \mathrm{N}$, acting upward on the crate.
Step 12Check reasonableness: Each kilogram weighs about $10\ \mathrm{N}$, so $75\ \mathrm{kg}$ should weigh roughly $750\ \mathrm{N}$. The answer $736\ \mathrm{N}$ agrees and carries force units.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of the crate
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the crate by cutting the cable. Two forces act on it: the cable tension $T$ pulling upward at the top of the crate, and the weight $W$ acting downward through the center $G$. List knowns and unknowns: $m = 75\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $T$. State the model: The crate is at rest, so it is in equilibrium. The cable is vertical and its own weight is neglected. Set axes and sign convention: $+y$ upward, $+x$ to the right. Write the weight law: $W = mg$. This is Newton's second law $F = ma$ with $a = g$; it converts a mass in kg into a force in N. Substitute numbers: $$W = (75\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2})$$ Compute the weight: $W = 735.75\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2} = 735.75\ \mathrm{N}$, since $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$. Sum forces in x: $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically because no force has a horizontal component. Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ T - W = 0$. Both forces share one vertical line of action through $G$, so $\sum M_G = 0$ is also satisfied automatically. Rearrange: $T = W$. State the result: $T = 735.75\ \mathrm{N} \approx 736\ \mathrm{N}$, acting upward on the crate. Check reasonableness: Each kilogram weighs about $10\ \mathrm{N}$, so $75\ \mathrm{kg}$ should weigh roughly $750\ \mathrm{N}$. The answer $736\ \mathrm{N}$ agrees and carries force units.
Problem 2
Ch. 1 — Converting a Moment from lb·ft to N·m
A torque wrench is set to tighten a bolt at $O$ to $M = 250\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$ and $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$, express this moment in SI units.
Torque wrench on a bolt
Express $M$ in $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Solution
339 N·m
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $M = 250\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft}$. Conversion factors: $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$, $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $M$ in $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Step 2Describe the plan: A moment is a force times a length, so its unit is a compound unit. Each base unit in it must be converted with its own factor.
Step 3Write the force factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}} = 1$.
Step 4Write the length factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}} = 1$.
Step 5Set up the conversion symbolically: $$M = (250\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft})\left(\frac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}}\right)\left(\frac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}}\right)$$
Step 6Cancel units: $\mathrm{lb}$ cancels $\mathrm{lb}$ and $\mathrm{ft}$ cancels $\mathrm{ft}$, leaving $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Step 7Convert the force part: $250(4.448) = 1112\ \mathrm{N\cdot ft}$.
Step 8Convert the length part: $1112(0.3048) = 338.94\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Step 9Round the final answer: Keep four figures in the intermediate value 338.94 and report three: $M = 339\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Step 10Check reasonableness: The combined factor is $4.448(0.3048) \approx 1.356$, so $1\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft} \approx 1.36\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$ and $250(1.36) \approx 340\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$. The result agrees and has units of force times length.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $M = 250\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft}$. Conversion factors: $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$, $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $M$ in $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$. Describe the plan: A moment is a force times a length, so its unit is a compound unit. Each base unit in it must be converted with its own factor. Write the force factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}} = 1$. Write the length factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}} = 1$. Set up the conversion symbolically: $$M = (250\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft})\left(\frac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}}\right)\left(\frac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}}\right)$$ Cancel units: $\mathrm{lb}$ cancels $\mathrm{lb}$ and $\mathrm{ft}$ cancels $\mathrm{ft}$, leaving $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$. Convert the force part: $250(4.448) = 1112\ \mathrm{N\cdot ft}$. Convert the length part: $1112(0.3048) = 338.94\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$. Round the final answer: Keep four figures in the intermediate value 338.94 and report three: $M = 339\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$. Check reasonableness: The combined factor is $4.448(0.3048) \approx 1.356$, so $1\ \mathrm{lb\cdot ft} \approx 1.36\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$ and $250(1.36) \approx 340\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$. The result agrees and has units of force times length.
Problem 3
Ch. 1 — Specific Weight Conversion and Slab Weight
A rectangular concrete floor slab measures $4\ \mathrm{m}$ by $3\ \mathrm{m}$ in plan and is $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ thick. A U.S. handbook lists the specific weight of the concrete as $\gamma = 150\ \mathrm{lb/ft^3}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$ and $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$, determine the weight $W$ of the slab in kilonewtons.
Concrete slab with its dimensions
Determine the slab weight $W$ in kN.
Solution
42.4 kN
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: Slab $4\ \mathrm{m} \times 3\ \mathrm{m} \times 0.15\ \mathrm{m}$; $\gamma = 150\ \mathrm{lb/ft^3}$; $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $W$ in kN.
Step 2State the model: The slab is a homogeneous rectangular prism, so weight equals specific weight times volume.
Step 3Describe the plan: The dimensions are SI but $\gamma$ is U.S. Customary. Convert $\gamma$ to $\mathrm{N/m^3}$ first so every quantity is in one system.
Step 4Convert the volume unit: The length factor is cubed because the unit is $\mathrm{ft^3}$: $1\ \mathrm{ft^3} = (0.3048\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 0.028317\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
Step 5Convert the force unit: $150\ \mathrm{lb} = 150(4.448) = 667.2\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 6Write the converted specific weight: $$\gamma = \frac{667.2\ \mathrm{N}}{0.028317\ \mathrm{m^3}}$$
Step 7Compute the specific weight: $\gamma = 23\,562\ \mathrm{N/m^3} = 23.56\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$.
Step 8Write the volume formula: $V = L\,b\,t$.
Step 9Compute the volume: $V = (4)(3)(0.15) = 1.800\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
Step 10Write the weight formula: $W = \gamma V$, which is dimensionally homogeneous: $(\mathrm{N/m^3})(\mathrm{m^3}) = \mathrm{N}$.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$W = (23.56\ \mathrm{kN/m^3})(1.800\ \mathrm{m^3}) = 42.41\ \mathrm{kN}$$
Step 12State the result: $W = 42.4\ \mathrm{kN}$, acting downward through the center of the slab.
Step 13Check reasonableness: Normal concrete is about $2400\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, giving $2400(9.81)(1.8) \approx 42\ \mathrm{kN}$. The converted value is consistent.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: Slab $4\ \mathrm{m} \times 3\ \mathrm{m} \times 0.15\ \mathrm{m}$; $\gamma = 150\ \mathrm{lb/ft^3}$; $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $W$ in kN. State the model: The slab is a homogeneous rectangular prism, so weight equals specific weight times volume. Describe the plan: The dimensions are SI but $\gamma$ is U.S. Customary. Convert $\gamma$ to $\mathrm{N/m^3}$ first so every quantity is in one system. Convert the volume unit: The length factor is cubed because the unit is $\mathrm{ft^3}$: $1\ \mathrm{ft^3} = (0.3048\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 0.028317\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Convert the force unit: $150\ \mathrm{lb} = 150(4.448) = 667.2\ \mathrm{N}$. Write the converted specific weight: $$\gamma = \frac{667.2\ \mathrm{N}}{0.028317\ \mathrm{m^3}}$$ Compute the specific weight: $\gamma = 23\,562\ \mathrm{N/m^3} = 23.56\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$. Write the volume formula: $V = L\,b\,t$. Compute the volume: $V = (4)(3)(0.15) = 1.800\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Write the weight formula: $W = \gamma V$, which is dimensionally homogeneous: $(\mathrm{N/m^3})(\mathrm{m^3}) = \mathrm{N}$. Substitute numbers: $$W = (23.56\ \mathrm{kN/m^3})(1.800\ \mathrm{m^3}) = 42.41\ \mathrm{kN}$$ State the result: $W = 42.4\ \mathrm{kN}$, acting downward through the center of the slab. Check reasonableness: Normal concrete is about $2400\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, giving $2400(9.81)(1.8) \approx 42\ \mathrm{kN}$. The converted value is consistent.
Problem 4
Ch. 1 — Converting a Force from Pounds to Newtons
A worker pushes horizontally on a loaded cart with a force of $P = 85\ \mathrm{lb}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$, express the force in SI units.
Horizontal push on a cart
Express $P$ in newtons.
Solution
378 N
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $P = 85\ \mathrm{lb}$; conversion factor $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$. Unknown: $P$ in N.
Step 2Identify the unit systems: The pound is the U.S. Customary unit of force; the newton is the SI unit of force. Both measure the same physical quantity, so a single factor converts one to the other.
Step 3Write the conversion factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}} = 1$.
Step 4Choose the orientation of the ratio: Newtons go on top and pounds on the bottom so that pounds cancel.
Step 5Set up the conversion symbolically: $$P = (85\ \mathrm{lb})\left(\frac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}}\right)$$
Step 6Cancel units: $\mathrm{lb}$ in the numerator cancels $\mathrm{lb}$ in the denominator, leaving N.
Step 7Multiply: $85(4.448) = 378.08\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 8Round the final answer: To three significant figures, $378.08 \rightarrow 378$.
Step 9State the result: $P = 378\ \mathrm{N}$, directed horizontally to the right.
Step 10Check reasonableness: One pound is a little under $4.5\ \mathrm{N}$, so $85\ \mathrm{lb}$ should be a little under $85(4.5) = 383\ \mathrm{N}$. The answer $378\ \mathrm{N}$ fits.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $P = 85\ \mathrm{lb}$; conversion factor $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$. Unknown: $P$ in N. Identify the unit systems: The pound is the U.S. Customary unit of force; the newton is the SI unit of force. Both measure the same physical quantity, so a single factor converts one to the other. Write the conversion factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}} = 1$. Choose the orientation of the ratio: Newtons go on top and pounds on the bottom so that pounds cancel. Set up the conversion symbolically: $$P = (85\ \mathrm{lb})\left(\frac{4.448\ \mathrm{N}}{1\ \mathrm{lb}}\right)$$ Cancel units: $\mathrm{lb}$ in the numerator cancels $\mathrm{lb}$ in the denominator, leaving N. Multiply: $85(4.448) = 378.08\ \mathrm{N}$. Round the final answer: To three significant figures, $378.08 \rightarrow 378$. State the result: $P = 378\ \mathrm{N}$, directed horizontally to the right. Check reasonableness: One pound is a little under $4.5\ \mathrm{N}$, so $85\ \mathrm{lb}$ should be a little under $85(4.5) = 383\ \mathrm{N}$. The answer $378\ \mathrm{N}$ fits.
Problem 5
Ch. 1 — SI Prefixes: Stress in a Wire
A straight steel wire of diameter $d = 2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ carries an axial tensile force $F = 4.2\ \mathrm{kN}$. The average normal stress is $\sigma = F/A$, where $A$ is the cross-sectional area. Determine $\sigma$ and express it in megapascals ($1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$).
Wire in tension with its circular cross-section
Determine the stress $\sigma$ in MPa.
Solution
856 MPa
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $d = 2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, $F = 4.2\ \mathrm{kN}$. Unknown: $\sigma$ in MPa.
Step 2State the model: The force acts along the wire axis and the stress is uniform over a circular cross-section.
Step 3Convert the force to base units: $F = 4.2\ \mathrm{kN} = 4.2(10^3)\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 4Convert the diameter to base units: $d = 2.5\ \mathrm{mm} = 2.5(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$, so the radius is $r = 1.25(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$.
Step 5Write the area formula: $A = \pi r^2$.
Step 6Substitute into the area: $$A = \pi\left[1.25(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}\right]^2$$
Step 7Compute the area: $A = 4.909(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The prefix is squared along with the number: $(10^{-3})^2 = 10^{-6}$.
Step 8Write the stress formula: $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$, with units $\mathrm{N/m^2} = \mathrm{Pa}$.
Step 9Substitute numbers: $$\sigma = \frac{4.2(10^3)\ \mathrm{N}}{4.909(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^2}}$$
Step 10Compute the stress: $\sigma = 855.6(10^{6})\ \mathrm{N/m^2} = 855.6(10^{6})\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
Step 11Apply the prefix: $10^6\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{MPa}$, so $\sigma = 855.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \approx 856\ \mathrm{MPa}$.
Step 12Check reasonableness: A shortcut is $\mathrm{N/mm^2} = \mathrm{MPa}$: $4200\ \mathrm{N} / 4.909\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 856\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Both routes agree.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $d = 2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, $F = 4.2\ \mathrm{kN}$. Unknown: $\sigma$ in MPa. State the model: The force acts along the wire axis and the stress is uniform over a circular cross-section. Convert the force to base units: $F = 4.2\ \mathrm{kN} = 4.2(10^3)\ \mathrm{N}$. Convert the diameter to base units: $d = 2.5\ \mathrm{mm} = 2.5(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$, so the radius is $r = 1.25(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$. Write the area formula: $A = \pi r^2$. Substitute into the area: $$A = \pi\left[1.25(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}\right]^2$$ Compute the area: $A = 4.909(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The prefix is squared along with the number: $(10^{-3})^2 = 10^{-6}$. Write the stress formula: $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$, with units $\mathrm{N/m^2} = \mathrm{Pa}$. Substitute numbers: $$\sigma = \frac{4.2(10^3)\ \mathrm{N}}{4.909(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^2}}$$ Compute the stress: $\sigma = 855.6(10^{6})\ \mathrm{N/m^2} = 855.6(10^{6})\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Apply the prefix: $10^6\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{MPa}$, so $\sigma = 855.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \approx 856\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Check reasonableness: A shortcut is $\mathrm{N/mm^2} = \mathrm{MPa}$: $4200\ \mathrm{N} / 4.909\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 856\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Both routes agree.
Problem 6
Ch. 1 — Mixed Prefixes in a Formula
The midspan deflection of a simply supported beam with a central load is $\delta = \dfrac{P L^3}{48 E I}$. For a beam with $P = 4.5\ \mathrm{kN}$, $L = 3.2\ \mathrm{m}$, $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa}$ and $I = 8.5(10^{6})\ \mathrm{mm^4}$, determine $\delta$ in millimetres.
Simply supported beam with a central load
Determine the deflection $\delta$ in mm.
Solution
1.81 mm
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $P = 4.5\ \mathrm{kN}$, $L = 3.2\ \mathrm{m}$, $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa}$, $I = 8.5(10^{6})\ \mathrm{mm^4}$. Unknown: $\delta$ in mm.
Step 2Describe the plan: The data mix the prefixes k, G and m. Convert everything to N and m, evaluate the formula, then convert the result to mm.
Step 3Convert the load: $P = 4.5\ \mathrm{kN} = 4.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 4Convert the modulus: $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa} = 200(10^{9})\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$.
Step 5Convert the moment of inertia: $1\ \mathrm{mm^4} = (10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m})^4 = 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m^4}$, so $I = 8.5(10^{6})(10^{-12}) = 8.5(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^4}$.
Step 6Check dimensional homogeneity: $\dfrac{(\mathrm{N})(\mathrm{m^3})}{(\mathrm{N/m^2})(\mathrm{m^4})} = \mathrm{m}$, a length, as a deflection must be.
Step 7Write the governing formula: $$\delta = \frac{P L^3}{48 E I}$$
Step 8Evaluate the numerator: $P L^3 = 4.5(10^{3})(3.2)^3 = 4.5(10^{3})(32.768) = 147.46(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^3}$.
Step 9Evaluate the denominator: $48 E I = 48\left[200(10^{9})\right]\left[8.5(10^{-6})\right] = 81.60(10^{6})\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2}$.
Step 10Divide: $$\delta = \frac{147.46(10^{3})}{81.60(10^{6})} = 1.807(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$$
Step 11Apply the prefix: $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{mm}$, so $\delta = 1.807\ \mathrm{mm} \approx 1.81\ \mathrm{mm}$ downward.
Step 12Check reasonableness: The deflection is about $L/1800$, a small fraction of the span, which is typical of a stiff steel beam.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $P = 4.5\ \mathrm{kN}$, $L = 3.2\ \mathrm{m}$, $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa}$, $I = 8.5(10^{6})\ \mathrm{mm^4}$. Unknown: $\delta$ in mm. Describe the plan: The data mix the prefixes k, G and m. Convert everything to N and m, evaluate the formula, then convert the result to mm. Convert the load: $P = 4.5\ \mathrm{kN} = 4.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}$. Convert the modulus: $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa} = 200(10^{9})\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$. Convert the moment of inertia: $1\ \mathrm{mm^4} = (10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m})^4 = 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m^4}$, so $I = 8.5(10^{6})(10^{-12}) = 8.5(10^{-6})\ \mathrm{m^4}$. Check dimensional homogeneity: $\dfrac{(\mathrm{N})(\mathrm{m^3})}{(\mathrm{N/m^2})(\mathrm{m^4})} = \mathrm{m}$, a length, as a deflection must be. Write the governing formula: $$\delta = \frac{P L^3}{48 E I}$$ Evaluate the numerator: $P L^3 = 4.5(10^{3})(3.2)^3 = 4.5(10^{3})(32.768) = 147.46(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^3}$. Evaluate the denominator: $48 E I = 48\left[200(10^{9})\right]\left[8.5(10^{-6})\right] = 81.60(10^{6})\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2}$. Divide: $$\delta = \frac{147.46(10^{3})}{81.60(10^{6})} = 1.807(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m}$$ Apply the prefix: $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{mm}$, so $\delta = 1.807\ \mathrm{mm} \approx 1.81\ \mathrm{mm}$ downward. Check reasonableness: The deflection is about $L/1800$, a small fraction of the span, which is typical of a stiff steel beam.
Problem 7
Ch. 1 — Mass from Weight
A shipping tag states that a steel beam weighs $W = 14.2\ \mathrm{kN}$. Taking $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, determine the mass of the beam in megagrams ($1\ \mathrm{Mg} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg}$).
Steel beam with its weight
Determine the mass $m$ in Mg.
Solution
1.45 Mg
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $W = 14.2\ \mathrm{kN}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $m$ in Mg.
Step 2Distinguish the quantities: Weight is a force (N); mass is a quantity of matter (kg). They are linked by Newton's second law.
Step 3Convert the weight to base units: $W = 14.2\ \mathrm{kN} = 14.2(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 4Write the governing equation: $W = mg$, which is $F = ma$ with $a = g$.
Step 5Rearrange for mass: $m = \dfrac{W}{g}$.
Step 6Substitute numbers: $$m = \frac{14.2(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}}{9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}}$$
Step 7Check the units: $\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \mathrm{kg}$.
Step 8Compute the mass: $m = 1447.5\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Step 9Apply the prefix: $1447.5\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.4475(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.4475\ \mathrm{Mg}$.
Step 10State the result: $m = 1.45\ \mathrm{Mg}$.
Step 11Check reasonableness: Dividing a weight in newtons by about 10 gives the mass in kilograms: $14\,200/10 \approx 1420\ \mathrm{kg}$, close to $1450\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $W = 14.2\ \mathrm{kN}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $m$ in Mg. Distinguish the quantities: Weight is a force (N); mass is a quantity of matter (kg). They are linked by Newton's second law. Convert the weight to base units: $W = 14.2\ \mathrm{kN} = 14.2(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}$. Write the governing equation: $W = mg$, which is $F = ma$ with $a = g$. Rearrange for mass: $m = \dfrac{W}{g}$. Substitute numbers: $$m = \frac{14.2(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N}}{9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}}$$ Check the units: $\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \mathrm{kg}$. Compute the mass: $m = 1447.5\ \mathrm{kg}$. Apply the prefix: $1447.5\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.4475(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.4475\ \mathrm{Mg}$. State the result: $m = 1.45\ \mathrm{Mg}$. Check reasonableness: Dividing a weight in newtons by about 10 gives the mass in kilograms: $14\,200/10 \approx 1420\ \mathrm{kg}$, close to $1450\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Problem 8
Ch. 1 — Weight Depends on Local Gravity
A rover of mass $m = 185\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on level ground. On Earth $g_E = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$; on the Moon $g_M = 1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Determine by how much the total normal force $N$ that the ground exerts on the rover decreases when the rover is moved from Earth to the Moon. Express the answer in kilonewtons.
Rover resting on level ground
Determine the decrease in normal force, $\Delta N = N_E - N_M$, in kN.
Solution
1.52 kN
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of the rover
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the rover from the ground. Two forces act: the weight $W$ downward through $G$ and the total normal force $N$ from the ground upward. The same diagram applies on Earth and on the Moon; only the size of $W$ changes.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $m = 185\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g_E = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $g_M = 1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $\Delta N = N_E - N_M$.
Step 3State the model: The rover is at rest on level ground, so it is in equilibrium. The mass is the same in both places; only $g$ differs.
Step 4Set axes and sign convention: $+y$ upward.
Step 5Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ N - W = 0$. There are no horizontal forces, so $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically.
Step 6Rearrange: $N = W = mg$.
Step 7Evaluate on Earth: $N_E = (185)(9.81) = 1814.9\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 8Evaluate on the Moon: $N_M = (185)(1.62) = 299.7\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 9Write the difference symbolically: $\Delta N = N_E - N_M = m(g_E - g_M)$.
Step 10Substitute numbers: $$\Delta N = 1814.9 - 299.7 = 1515.2\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 11Apply the prefix: $\Delta N = 1.5152(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 1.52\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 12Check reasonableness: Lunar gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so about five sixths of the Earth weight should disappear: $\tfrac{5}{6}(1815) \approx 1510\ \mathrm{N}$. The result agrees.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of the rover
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the rover from the ground. Two forces act: the weight $W$ downward through $G$ and the total normal force $N$ from the ground upward. The same diagram applies on Earth and on the Moon; only the size of $W$ changes. List knowns and unknowns: $m = 185\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g_E = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $g_M = 1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $\Delta N = N_E - N_M$. State the model: The rover is at rest on level ground, so it is in equilibrium. The mass is the same in both places; only $g$ differs. Set axes and sign convention: $+y$ upward. Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ N - W = 0$. There are no horizontal forces, so $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically. Rearrange: $N = W = mg$. Evaluate on Earth: $N_E = (185)(9.81) = 1814.9\ \mathrm{N}$. Evaluate on the Moon: $N_M = (185)(1.62) = 299.7\ \mathrm{N}$. Write the difference symbolically: $\Delta N = N_E - N_M = m(g_E - g_M)$. Substitute numbers: $$\Delta N = 1814.9 - 299.7 = 1515.2\ \mathrm{N}$$ Apply the prefix: $\Delta N = 1.5152(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 1.52\ \mathrm{kN}$. Check reasonableness: Lunar gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so about five sixths of the Earth weight should disappear: $\tfrac{5}{6}(1815) \approx 1510\ \mathrm{N}$. The result agrees.
Problem 9
Ch. 1 — Contact Pressure with Squared Unit Conversion
A truck weighing $W = 6500\ \mathrm{lb}$ is parked on level pavement with its weight shared equally by four tires. Each tire touches the pavement over a rectangular contact patch $8\ \mathrm{in}$ by $6\ \mathrm{in}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$ and $1\ \mathrm{in} = 0.0254\ \mathrm{m}$, determine the average contact pressure $p$ under one tire in kilopascals.
Truck on four tires and one contact patch
Determine the contact pressure $p$ in kPa.
Solution
233 kPa
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of the truck
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the truck from the pavement. The weight $W$ acts downward through $G$, and the pavement pushes up on each of the four tires with a normal force $N$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $W = 6500\ \mathrm{lb}$; four tires sharing the load equally; patch $8\ \mathrm{in} \times 6\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$; $1\ \mathrm{in} = 0.0254\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $p$ in kPa.
Step 3State the model: The truck is at rest on level ground and the pressure is uniform over each contact patch.
Step 4Convert the weight: $W = 6500(4.448) = 28\,912\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 5Sum forces in y: With $+y$ upward, $\sum F_y = 0:\ 4N - W = 0$. No horizontal forces act, so $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically.
Step 6Solve for the force on one tire: $N = \dfrac{W}{4} = \dfrac{28\,912}{4} = 7228\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 7Compute the patch area in the given units: $A = (8)(6) = 48\ \mathrm{in^2}$.
Step 8Convert the area: The length factor is squared: $1\ \mathrm{in^2} = (0.0254\ \mathrm{m})^2 = 6.4516(10^{-4})\ \mathrm{m^2}$, so $A = 48\left[6.4516(10^{-4})\right] = 0.030968\ \mathrm{m^2}$.
Step 9Write the pressure formula: $p = \dfrac{N}{A}$, with units $\mathrm{N/m^2} = \mathrm{Pa}$.
Step 10Substitute numbers: $$p = \frac{7228\ \mathrm{N}}{0.030968\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 233.4(10^{3})\ \mathrm{Pa}$$
Step 11Apply the prefix: $p = 233.4\ \mathrm{kPa} \approx 233\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
Step 12Check reasonableness: In U.S. units the pressure is $1625\ \mathrm{lb}/48\ \mathrm{in^2} = 33.9\ \mathrm{psi}$, a typical tire inflation pressure, and $33.9\ \mathrm{psi} \approx 233\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of the truck
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the truck from the pavement. The weight $W$ acts downward through $G$, and the pavement pushes up on each of the four tires with a normal force $N$. List knowns and unknowns: $W = 6500\ \mathrm{lb}$; four tires sharing the load equally; patch $8\ \mathrm{in} \times 6\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$; $1\ \mathrm{in} = 0.0254\ \mathrm{m}$. Solve for the force on one tire: $N = \dfrac{W}{4} = \dfrac{28\,912}{4} = 7228\ \mathrm{N}$. Compute the patch area in the given units: $A = (8)(6) = 48\ \mathrm{in^2}$. Convert the area: The length factor is squared: $1\ \mathrm{in^2} = (0.0254\ \mathrm{m})^2 = 6.4516(10^{-4})\ \mathrm{m^2}$, so $A = 48\left[6.4516(10^{-4})\right] = 0.030968\ \mathrm{m^2}$. Write the pressure formula: $p = \dfrac{N}{A}$, with units $\mathrm{N/m^2} = \mathrm{Pa}$. Substitute numbers: $$p = \frac{7228\ \mathrm{N}}{0.030968\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 233.4(10^{3})\ \mathrm{Pa}$$ Apply the prefix: $p = 233.4\ \mathrm{kPa} \approx 233\ \mathrm{kPa}$. Check reasonableness: In U.S. units the pressure is $1625\ \mathrm{lb}/48\ \mathrm{in^2} = 33.9\ \mathrm{psi}$, a typical tire inflation pressure, and $33.9\ \mathrm{psi} \approx 233\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
Problem 10
Ch. 1 — Converting Feet and Inches to Metres
A set of U.S. drawings gives the span of a roof beam between supports $A$ and $B$ as $18\ \mathrm{ft}\ 9\ \mathrm{in}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 12\ \mathrm{in}$ and $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$, express the span $L$ in metres.
Roof beam span between two supports
Express the span $L$ in metres.
Solution
5.72 m
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $L = 18\ \mathrm{ft}\ 9\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 12\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $L$ in m.
Step 2Describe the plan: The length is given in two different units. Combine them into a single unit (feet) before converting to metres.
Step 3Write the inch-to-foot factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{ft}}{12\ \mathrm{in}} = 1$.
Step 4Convert the inches: $9\ \mathrm{in}\left(\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{ft}}{12\ \mathrm{in}}\right) = 0.75\ \mathrm{ft}$.
Step 5Add the lengths in feet: $L = 18 + 0.75 = 18.75\ \mathrm{ft}$. Only quantities with the same unit can be added.
Step 6Write the foot-to-metre factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}} = 1$.
Step 7Set up the conversion: $$L = (18.75\ \mathrm{ft})\left(\frac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}}\right)$$
Step 8Cancel units: $\mathrm{ft}$ cancels, leaving m.
Step 9Multiply: $L = 5.715\ \mathrm{m}$.
Step 10Round the final answer: The fourth digit is 5. Rounding to three significant figures by the even-digit rule keeps the preceding digit even, giving $L = 5.72\ \mathrm{m}$.
Step 11Check reasonableness: A foot is a little less than a third of a metre, so $18.75\ \mathrm{ft}$ should be a little under $6.25\ \mathrm{m}$. The answer $5.72\ \mathrm{m}$ fits.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $L = 18\ \mathrm{ft}\ 9\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 12\ \mathrm{in}$; $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 0.3048\ \mathrm{m}$. Unknown: $L$ in m. Convert the inches: $9\ \mathrm{in}\left(\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{ft}}{12\ \mathrm{in}}\right) = 0.75\ \mathrm{ft}$. Add the lengths in feet: $L = 18 + 0.75 = 18.75\ \mathrm{ft}$. Only quantities with the same unit can be added. Write the foot-to-metre factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}} = 1$. Set up the conversion: $$L = (18.75\ \mathrm{ft})\left(\frac{0.3048\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{ft}}\right)$$ Cancel units: $\mathrm{ft}$ cancels, leaving m. Multiply: $L = 5.715\ \mathrm{m}$. Problem 11
Ch. 1 — Newton's Second Law with a Speed Conversion
A car of mass $m = 1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ starts from rest and accelerates uniformly along a straight level road, reaching $90\ \mathrm{km/h}$ in $t = 8\ \mathrm{s}$. Determine the net horizontal force $F$ required, in kilonewtons.
Car accelerating along a level road
Determine the net force $F$ in kN.
Solution
3.75 kN
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of the car
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the car. Vertically, the weight $W$ acts down and the road's normal force $N$ acts up; these balance. Horizontally, a single net force $F$ acts in the direction of motion.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $m = 1200\ \mathrm{kg}$, $v_0 = 0$, $v = 90\ \mathrm{km/h}$, $t = 8\ \mathrm{s}$. Unknown: $F$ in kN.
Step 3State the model: The acceleration is constant and the motion is along a straight level road, so only the $x$ direction matters.
Step 4Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ in the direction of travel.
Step 5Write the speed conversion as ratios equal to one: $\dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}} = 1$ and $\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{h}}{3600\ \mathrm{s}} = 1$.
Step 6Convert the speed: $$v = 90\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{h}}\left(\frac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}\right)\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{h}}{3600\ \mathrm{s}}\right) = 25.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$$
Step 7Write the acceleration formula: For uniform acceleration from rest, $a = \dfrac{v - v_0}{t}$.
Step 8Compute the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{25.00 - 0}{8} = 3.125\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Step 9Write Newton's second law: $\sum F_x = ma$, so $F = ma$. This law ties the four basic quantities force, mass, length and time together.
Step 10Substitute numbers: $$F = (1200\ \mathrm{kg})(3.125\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 3750\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2} = 3750\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 11Apply the prefix: $F = 3.75(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 3.75\ \mathrm{kN}$, in the direction of motion.
Step 12Check reasonableness: The acceleration is about one third of $g$, so the force should be about one third of the car's weight, $\tfrac{1}{3}(11.8\ \mathrm{kN}) \approx 3.9\ \mathrm{kN}$. The result is consistent.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of the car
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the car. Vertically, the weight $W$ acts down and the road's normal force $N$ acts up; these balance. Horizontally, a single net force $F$ acts in the direction of motion. List knowns and unknowns: $m = 1200\ \mathrm{kg}$, $v_0 = 0$, $v = 90\ \mathrm{km/h}$, $t = 8\ \mathrm{s}$. Unknown: $F$ in kN. State the model: The acceleration is constant and the motion is along a straight level road, so only the $x$ direction matters. Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ in the direction of travel. Write the speed conversion as ratios equal to one: $\dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}} = 1$ and $\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{h}}{3600\ \mathrm{s}} = 1$. Convert the speed: $$v = 90\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{h}}\left(\frac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}\right)\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{h}}{3600\ \mathrm{s}}\right) = 25.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$$ Write the acceleration formula: For uniform acceleration from rest, $a = \dfrac{v - v_0}{t}$. Compute the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{25.00 - 0}{8} = 3.125\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Write Newton's second law: $\sum F_x = ma$, so $F = ma$. This law ties the four basic quantities force, mass, length and time together. Substitute numbers: $$F = (1200\ \mathrm{kg})(3.125\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 3750\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2} = 3750\ \mathrm{N}$$ Apply the prefix: $F = 3.75(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 3.75\ \mathrm{kN}$, in the direction of motion. Check reasonableness: The acceleration is about one third of $g$, so the force should be about one third of the car's weight, $\tfrac{1}{3}(11.8\ \mathrm{kN}) \approx 3.9\ \mathrm{kN}$. The result is consistent.
Problem 12
Ch. 1 — Effect of Rounding Intermediate Values
A weight $W = 1375\ \mathrm{N}$ hangs from a ring at $C$ supported by two identical cables $CA$ and $CB$, each inclined at $\theta = 17.5^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. A student rounds each intermediate value to two significant figures before computing the cable tension $T$. Determine the percent error in the student's tension compared with the value obtained by carrying at least four significant figures.
Weight supported by two symmetric cables
Determine the percent error in the student's value of $T$.
Solution
2.06 %
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of ring C
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the ring $C$. Three forces act on it: cable tension $T$ along $CA$ (up and to the left at $17.5^{\circ}$ above horizontal), cable tension $T$ along $CB$ (up and to the right at $17.5^{\circ}$), and the weight $W$ straight down.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $W = 1375\ \mathrm{N}$, $\theta = 17.5^{\circ}$. Unknown: percent error between the tension found with two-figure intermediates and the tension found with four-figure intermediates.
Step 3State the model: The ring is a particle in equilibrium; the cables are identical and symmetric, so they carry the same tension $T$.
Step 4Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward.
Step 5Resolve the tension in CA: $x$-component $-T\cos\theta$, $y$-component $+T\sin\theta$.
Step 6Resolve the tension in CB: $x$-component $+T\cos\theta$, $y$-component $+T\sin\theta$.
Step 7Sum forces in x: $\sum F_x = 0:\ T\cos\theta - T\cos\theta = 0$, which confirms the tensions are equal. All three forces pass through $C$, so $\sum M_C = 0$ is satisfied automatically.
Step 8Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ 2T\sin\theta - W = 0$.
Step 9Rearrange: $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$.
Step 10Evaluate carefully: With $\sin 17.5^{\circ} = 0.3007$, $$T = \frac{1375}{2(0.3007)} = 2286\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 11Evaluate the student's way: Rounding to two figures gives $W \rightarrow 1400\ \mathrm{N}$ and $\sin\theta \rightarrow 0.30$, so $$T_s = \frac{1400}{2(0.30)} = 2333\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 12Write the percent-error formula: $\%\,\text{error} = \dfrac{T_s - T}{T}(100)$.
Step 13Compute the error: $\dfrac{2333 - 2286}{2286}(100) = 2.06\ \%$ (using unrounded values 2333.3 and 2286.3).
Step 14Interpret the result: Early rounding produced an error above $2\ \%$, worse than the roughly $1\ \%$ accuracy that a three-figure answer implies. Carry at least four figures in intermediate steps and round only the final answer.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of ring C
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the ring $C$. Three forces act on it: cable tension $T$ along $CA$ (up and to the left at $17.5^{\circ}$ above horizontal), cable tension $T$ along $CB$ (up and to the right at $17.5^{\circ}$), and the weight $W$ straight down. List knowns and unknowns: $W = 1375\ \mathrm{N}$, $\theta = 17.5^{\circ}$. Unknown: percent error between the tension found with two-figure intermediates and the tension found with four-figure intermediates. State the model: The ring is a particle in equilibrium; the cables are identical and symmetric, so they carry the same tension $T$. Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward. Resolve the tension in CA: $x$-component $-T\cos\theta$, $y$-component $+T\sin\theta$. Resolve the tension in CB: $x$-component $+T\cos\theta$, $y$-component $+T\sin\theta$. Sum forces in x: $\sum F_x = 0:\ T\cos\theta - T\cos\theta = 0$, which confirms the tensions are equal. All three forces pass through $C$, so $\sum M_C = 0$ is satisfied automatically. Sum forces in y: $\sum F_y = 0:\ 2T\sin\theta - W = 0$. Rearrange: $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$. Evaluate carefully: With $\sin 17.5^{\circ} = 0.3007$, $$T = \frac{1375}{2(0.3007)} = 2286\ \mathrm{N}$$ Evaluate the student's way: Rounding to two figures gives $W \rightarrow 1400\ \mathrm{N}$ and $\sin\theta \rightarrow 0.30$, so $$T_s = \frac{1400}{2(0.30)} = 2333\ \mathrm{N}$$ Write the percent-error formula: $\%\,\text{error} = \dfrac{T_s - T}{T}(100)$. Compute the error: $\dfrac{2333 - 2286}{2286}(100) = 2.06\ \%$ (using unrounded values 2333.3 and 2286.3). Interpret the result: Early rounding produced an error above $2\ \%$, worse than the roughly $1\ \%$ accuracy that a three-figure answer implies. Carry at least four figures in intermediate steps and round only the final answer.
Problem 13
Ch. 1 — Converting Mass from Slugs to Kilograms
The nameplate on an imported air compressor lists its mass as $12.5\ \mathrm{slug}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{slug} = 14.59\ \mathrm{kg}$, express the mass $m$ in SI units.
Air compressor with its nameplate mass
Express the mass $m$ in kilograms.
Solution
182 kg
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $m = 12.5\ \mathrm{slug}$; conversion factor $1\ \mathrm{slug} = 14.59\ \mathrm{kg}$. Unknown: $m$ in kg.
Step 2Identify the unit systems: In the U.S. Customary system force (lb), length (ft) and time (s) are base units and mass is derived from $F = ma$: $1\ \mathrm{slug} = 1\ \mathrm{lb\cdot s^2/ft}$.
Step 3Contrast with SI: In SI mass (kg), length (m) and time (s) are base units and force is derived: $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$.
Step 4Write the conversion factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{14.59\ \mathrm{kg}}{1\ \mathrm{slug}} = 1$.
Step 5Choose the orientation of the ratio: Kilograms on top and slugs on the bottom so that slugs cancel.
Step 6Set up the conversion: $$m = (12.5\ \mathrm{slug})\left(\frac{14.59\ \mathrm{kg}}{1\ \mathrm{slug}}\right)$$
Step 7Cancel units: $\mathrm{slug}$ cancels, leaving kg.
Step 8Multiply: $m = 182.4\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Step 9Round the final answer: To three significant figures, $m = 182\ \mathrm{kg}$. The symbol is written kg, never kgs.
Step 10Check reasonableness: The compressor weighs $12.5(32.2) \approx 403\ \mathrm{lb}$ on Earth, and $403\ \mathrm{lb}$ is about $1790\ \mathrm{N}$, which corresponds to $1790/9.81 \approx 182\ \mathrm{kg}$. The two routes agree.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $m = 12.5\ \mathrm{slug}$; conversion factor $1\ \mathrm{slug} = 14.59\ \mathrm{kg}$. Unknown: $m$ in kg. Identify the unit systems: In the U.S. Customary system force (lb), length (ft) and time (s) are base units and mass is derived from $F = ma$: $1\ \mathrm{slug} = 1\ \mathrm{lb\cdot s^2/ft}$. Contrast with SI: In SI mass (kg), length (m) and time (s) are base units and force is derived: $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$. Write the conversion factor as a ratio equal to one: $\dfrac{14.59\ \mathrm{kg}}{1\ \mathrm{slug}} = 1$. Choose the orientation of the ratio: Kilograms on top and slugs on the bottom so that slugs cancel. Set up the conversion: $$m = (12.5\ \mathrm{slug})\left(\frac{14.59\ \mathrm{kg}}{1\ \mathrm{slug}}\right)$$ Cancel units: $\mathrm{slug}$ cancels, leaving kg. Multiply: $m = 182.4\ \mathrm{kg}$. Round the final answer: To three significant figures, $m = 182\ \mathrm{kg}$. The symbol is written kg, never kgs. Check reasonableness: The compressor weighs $12.5(32.2) \approx 403\ \mathrm{lb}$ on Earth, and $403\ \mathrm{lb}$ is about $1790\ \mathrm{N}$, which corresponds to $1790/9.81 \approx 182\ \mathrm{kg}$. The two routes agree.
Problem 14
Ch. 1 — Interpret, Plan, Execute: Load per Column
A rectangular floor slab $9.5\ \mathrm{m}$ by $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ has a mass of $21\ \mathrm{Mg}$ and carries a uniform floor loading of $4.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$ over its whole area. The slab is supported by six columns that share the total load equally. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Determine the force $R$ carried by each column in kilonewtons.
Floor slab on six columns
Determine the force $R$ in each column in kN.
Solution
79.9 kN
Free-body diagram
Free-body diagram of the slab
Step 1Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the slab from the columns. Acting downward are the slab weight $W$ and the resultant $F_L$ of the floor loading; acting upward are six equal column forces $R$.
Step 2Interpret: Given: slab $9.5\ \mathrm{m} \times 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$, mass $21\ \mathrm{Mg}$, loading $4.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$, six equally loaded columns, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: $R$ in kN.
Step 3Plan: (1) Turn the pressure into a force using the area. (2) Turn the mass into a weight. (3) Add the two downward forces. (4) Use vertical equilibrium to split the total among six columns.
Step 4Compute the area: $A = (9.5)(6.0) = 57.0\ \mathrm{m^2}$.
Step 5Write the loading resultant: $F_L = pA$, with $1\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1\ \mathrm{kN/m^2}$.
Step 6Compute the loading resultant: $F_L = (4.8\ \mathrm{kN/m^2})(57.0\ \mathrm{m^2}) = 273.6\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 7Convert the mass: $21\ \mathrm{Mg} = 21(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Step 8Compute the slab weight: $W = mg = 21(10^{3})(9.81) = 206.0(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 206.0\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 9Sum forces in y: With $+y$ upward, $\sum F_y = 0:\ 6R - F_L - W = 0$. No horizontal forces act, so $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically.
Step 10Rearrange: $R = \dfrac{F_L + W}{6}$.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$R = \frac{273.6 + 206.0}{6} = \frac{479.6}{6} = 79.94\ \mathrm{kN}$$
Step 12State the result: $R = 79.9\ \mathrm{kN}$, compression in each column.
Step 13Reflect: The total load of about $480\ \mathrm{kN}$ over six columns is about $80\ \mathrm{kN}$ each, and both terms were in kN before they were added, so the units are consistent.
Worked Solution
Free-body diagram of the slab
Draw the free-body diagram: Isolate the slab from the columns. Acting downward are the slab weight $W$ and the resultant $F_L$ of the floor loading; acting upward are six equal column forces $R$. Interpret: Given: slab $9.5\ \mathrm{m} \times 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$, mass $21\ \mathrm{Mg}$, loading $4.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$, six equally loaded columns, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: $R$ in kN. Plan: (1) Turn the pressure into a force using the area. (2) Turn the mass into a weight. (3) Add the two downward forces. (4) Use vertical equilibrium to split the total among six columns. Compute the area: $A = (9.5)(6.0) = 57.0\ \mathrm{m^2}$. Write the loading resultant: $F_L = pA$, with $1\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1\ \mathrm{kN/m^2}$. Compute the loading resultant: $F_L = (4.8\ \mathrm{kN/m^2})(57.0\ \mathrm{m^2}) = 273.6\ \mathrm{kN}$. Convert the mass: $21\ \mathrm{Mg} = 21(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg}$. Compute the slab weight: $W = mg = 21(10^{3})(9.81) = 206.0(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N} = 206.0\ \mathrm{kN}$. Sum forces in y: With $+y$ upward, $\sum F_y = 0:\ 6R - F_L - W = 0$. No horizontal forces act, so $\sum F_x = 0$ is satisfied identically. Rearrange: $R = \dfrac{F_L + W}{6}$. Substitute numbers: $$R = \frac{273.6 + 206.0}{6} = \frac{479.6}{6} = 79.94\ \mathrm{kN}$$ State the result: $R = 79.9\ \mathrm{kN}$, compression in each column. Reflect: The total load of about $480\ \mathrm{kN}$ over six columns is about $80\ \mathrm{kN}$ each, and both terms were in kN before they were added, so the units are consistent.
Problem 15
Ch. 1 — Weight of a Hollow Pipe from Density
A hollow steel pipe has an outside diameter of $114\ \mathrm{mm}$, a wall thickness of $6\ \mathrm{mm}$ and a length of $4.5\ \mathrm{m}$. The density of steel is $\rho = 7.85\ \mathrm{Mg/m^3}$. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Determine the weight $W$ of the pipe in newtons.
Hollow pipe with its cross-section
Determine the weight $W$ of the pipe in N.
Solution
705 N
Step 1List knowns and unknowns: $d_o = 114\ \mathrm{mm}$, $t = 6\ \mathrm{mm}$, $L = 4.5\ \mathrm{m}$, $\rho = 7.85\ \mathrm{Mg/m^3}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $W$ in N.
Step 2State the model: The pipe is a uniform hollow cylinder, so its volume is the ring-shaped cross-sectional area times the length.
Step 3Find the inside diameter: The wall is removed from both sides: $d_i = d_o - 2t = 114 - 2(6) = 102\ \mathrm{mm}$.
Step 4Convert the diameters: $d_o = 0.114\ \mathrm{m}$ and $d_i = 0.102\ \mathrm{m}$.
Step 5Convert the density: $\rho = 7.85\ \mathrm{Mg/m^3} = 7.85(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 7850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
Step 6Write the area formula: $A = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(d_o^2 - d_i^2\right)$.
Step 7Compute the area: $$A = \frac{\pi}{4}\left(0.114^2 - 0.102^2\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.012996 - 0.010404) = 2.0358(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^2}$$
Step 8Compute the volume: $V = AL = 2.0358(10^{-3})(4.5) = 9.161(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
Step 9Compute the mass: $m = \rho V = (7850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})\left[9.161(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^3}\right] = 71.91\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Step 10Write the weight law: $W = mg$.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$W = (71.91\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 705.5\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 12State the result: $W = 705\ \mathrm{N}$ (from the unrounded value $705.47\ \mathrm{N}$), acting downward at midlength.
Step 13Check reasonableness: The mass per metre is $71.91/4.5 \approx 16\ \mathrm{kg/m}$, in line with tabulated values for a 114-mm pipe with a 6-mm wall.
Worked Solution
List knowns and unknowns: $d_o = 114\ \mathrm{mm}$, $t = 6\ \mathrm{mm}$, $L = 4.5\ \mathrm{m}$, $\rho = 7.85\ \mathrm{Mg/m^3}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Unknown: $W$ in N. State the model: The pipe is a uniform hollow cylinder, so its volume is the ring-shaped cross-sectional area times the length. Find the inside diameter: The wall is removed from both sides: $d_i = d_o - 2t = 114 - 2(6) = 102\ \mathrm{mm}$. Convert the diameters: $d_o = 0.114\ \mathrm{m}$ and $d_i = 0.102\ \mathrm{m}$. Convert the density: $\rho = 7.85\ \mathrm{Mg/m^3} = 7.85(10^{3})\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 7850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Write the area formula: $A = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(d_o^2 - d_i^2\right)$. Compute the area: $$A = \frac{\pi}{4}\left(0.114^2 - 0.102^2\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.012996 - 0.010404) = 2.0358(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^2}$$ Compute the volume: $V = AL = 2.0358(10^{-3})(4.5) = 9.161(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Compute the mass: $m = \rho V = (7850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})\left[9.161(10^{-3})\ \mathrm{m^3}\right] = 71.91\ \mathrm{kg}$. Write the weight law: $W = mg$. Substitute numbers: $$W = (71.91\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 705.5\ \mathrm{N}$$ State the result: $W = 705\ \mathrm{N}$ (from the unrounded value $705.47\ \mathrm{N}$), acting downward at midlength. Check reasonableness: The mass per metre is $71.91/4.5 \approx 16\ \mathrm{kg/m}$, in line with tabulated values for a 114-mm pipe with a 6-mm wall.
Problem 16
Ch. 2 — Rectangular Component of a 2-D Force
A cable attached to an eyebolt at $O$ pulls with a force $F = 450\ \mathrm{N}$ directed up and to the left, at $40^{\circ}$ above the negative $x$-axis. Determine the $x$-component of the force, $F_x$.
Cable force on an eyebolt
Determine $F_x$.
Solution
-345 N
Free-body diagram
Component triangle for F
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Place the tail of $F$ at $O$ and draw it up and to the left at $40^{\circ}$ above the negative $x$-axis. Drop a perpendicular to the $x$-axis to form a right triangle with legs $F_x$ and $F_y$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F = 450\ \mathrm{N}$, angle $40^{\circ}$ measured from the negative $x$-axis. Unknown: $F_x$.
Step 3Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward; unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
Step 4Identify the triangle sides: The $40^{\circ}$ angle lies between $F$ and the $x$-axis, so the $x$ leg is adjacent to the angle and the $y$ leg is opposite.
Step 5Write the magnitude of the x leg: $|F_x| = F\cos 40^{\circ}$, because cosine gives the adjacent side.
Step 6Assign the sign: The force points to the left, the negative $x$ direction, so $F_x = -F\cos 40^{\circ}$.
Step 7Substitute numbers: $$F_x = -(450\ \mathrm{N})\cos 40^{\circ}$$
Step 8Evaluate the cosine: $\cos 40^{\circ} = 0.7660$.
Step 9Compute: $F_x = -(450)(0.7660) = -344.7\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 10State the result: $F_x = -345\ \mathrm{N}$, that is, $345\ \mathrm{N}$ acting to the left.
Step 11Check reasonableness: The companion component is $F_y = 450\sin 40^{\circ} = 289.3\ \mathrm{N}$, and $\sqrt{344.7^2 + 289.3^2} = 450\ \mathrm{N}$ recovers the original magnitude.
Worked Solution
Component triangle for F
Draw the vector sketch: Place the tail of $F$ at $O$ and draw it up and to the left at $40^{\circ}$ above the negative $x$-axis. Drop a perpendicular to the $x$-axis to form a right triangle with legs $F_x$ and $F_y$. List knowns and unknowns: $F = 450\ \mathrm{N}$, angle $40^{\circ}$ measured from the negative $x$-axis. Unknown: $F_x$. Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward; unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. Identify the triangle sides: The $40^{\circ}$ angle lies between $F$ and the $x$-axis, so the $x$ leg is adjacent to the angle and the $y$ leg is opposite. Write the magnitude of the x leg: $|F_x| = F\cos 40^{\circ}$, because cosine gives the adjacent side. Assign the sign: The force points to the left, the negative $x$ direction, so $F_x = -F\cos 40^{\circ}$. Substitute numbers: $$F_x = -(450\ \mathrm{N})\cos 40^{\circ}$$ Evaluate the cosine: $\cos 40^{\circ} = 0.7660$. Compute: $F_x = -(450)(0.7660) = -344.7\ \mathrm{N}$. State the result: $F_x = -345\ \mathrm{N}$, that is, $345\ \mathrm{N}$ acting to the left. Check reasonableness: The companion component is $F_y = 450\sin 40^{\circ} = 289.3\ \mathrm{N}$, and $\sqrt{344.7^2 + 289.3^2} = 450\ \mathrm{N}$ recovers the original magnitude.
Problem 17
Ch. 2 — Parallelogram Law: Resultant of Two Forces
Two ropes pull on a ring at $O$. Force $F_1 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ acts at $30^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis and force $F_2 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ acts at $105^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Using the parallelogram law and trigonometry, determine the magnitude of the resultant force $F_R$ in kilonewtons.
Two rope forces on a ring
Determine the magnitude $F_R$ in kN.
Solution
1.12 kN
Free-body diagram
Tip-to-tail force triangle
Step 1Draw the force triangle: Draw $F_1$ from $O$, then place the tail of $F_2$ at the tip of $F_1$ (tip to tail). The resultant $F_R$ runs from $O$ to the tip of $F_2$. This triangle is half of the parallelogram.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ at $30^{\circ}$, $F_2 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ at $105^{\circ}$. Unknown: $F_R$.
Step 3State the rule: Forces are vectors, so they add by the parallelogram law, not by simple arithmetic.
Step 4Find the angle between the forces: $105^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} = 75^{\circ}$.
Step 5Find the interior angle of the triangle: In the tip-to-tail triangle the angle between the sides $F_1$ and $F_2$ is the supplement, $180^{\circ} - 75^{\circ} = 105^{\circ}$. This angle is opposite $F_R$.
Step 6Write the law of cosines: $F_R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 - 2F_1F_2\cos 105^{\circ}$. It applies because two sides and the included angle are known.
Step 7Substitute numbers: $$F_R^2 = 600^2 + 800^2 - 2(600)(800)\cos 105^{\circ}$$
Step 8Evaluate the cosine term: $\cos 105^{\circ} = -0.2588$, so $-2(600)(800)(-0.2588) = +248.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N^2}$.
Step 9Add the terms: $F_R^2 = 360.0(10^{3}) + 640.0(10^{3}) + 248.5(10^{3}) = 1248.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N^2}$.
Step 10Take the square root: $F_R = \sqrt{1248.5(10^{3})} = 1117\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 11State the result: $F_R = 1.12\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 12Check reasonableness: The resultant must lie between $|F_2 - F_1| = 200\ \mathrm{N}$ and $F_1 + F_2 = 1400\ \mathrm{N}$. Because the forces are less than $90^{\circ}$ apart, it exceeds $\sqrt{600^2 + 800^2} = 1000\ \mathrm{N}$, as found.
Worked Solution
Tip-to-tail force triangle
Draw the force triangle: Draw $F_1$ from $O$, then place the tail of $F_2$ at the tip of $F_1$ (tip to tail). The resultant $F_R$ runs from $O$ to the tip of $F_2$. This triangle is half of the parallelogram. List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ at $30^{\circ}$, $F_2 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ at $105^{\circ}$. Unknown: $F_R$. This angle is opposite $F_R$. Write the law of cosines: $F_R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 - 2F_1F_2\cos 105^{\circ}$. It applies because two sides and the included angle are known. Substitute numbers: $$F_R^2 = 600^2 + 800^2 - 2(600)(800)\cos 105^{\circ}$$ Evaluate the cosine term: $\cos 105^{\circ} = -0.2588$, so $-2(600)(800)(-0.2588) = +248.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N^2}$. Add the terms: $F_R^2 = 360.0(10^{3}) + 640.0(10^{3}) + 248.5(10^{3}) = 1248.5(10^{3})\ \mathrm{N^2}$. Take the square root: $F_R = \sqrt{1248.5(10^{3})} = 1117\ \mathrm{N}$. State the result: $F_R = 1.12\ \mathrm{kN}$. Check reasonableness: The resultant must lie between $|F_2 - F_1| = 200\ \mathrm{N}$ and $F_1 + F_2 = 1400\ \mathrm{N}$. Because the forces are less than $90^{\circ}$ apart, it exceeds $\sqrt{600^2 + 800^2} = 1000\ \mathrm{N}$, as found.
Problem 18
Ch. 2 — Resolving a Force Along Non-Perpendicular Axes
A force $F = 2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$ acts on a gusset plate at $O$. The $u$-axis is horizontal and points to the right. The force is directed at $40^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from the positive $u$-axis, and the positive $v$-axis is directed at $105^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from the positive $u$-axis. Resolve $F$ into components along the $u$ and $v$ axes and determine the magnitude of the component $F_u$.
Force with oblique u and v axes
Determine the magnitude of $F_u$.
Solution
2.35 kN
Free-body diagram
Component triangle along u and v
Step 1Draw the parallelogram: From the tip of $F$ draw one line parallel to the $u$-axis and one parallel to the $v$-axis. They cut the axes at the tips of $F_u$ and $F_v$, forming a parallelogram with $F$ as its diagonal.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F = 2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$; angle from $u$ to $F$ is $40^{\circ}$; angle from $u$ to $v$ is $105^{\circ}$. Unknown: $F_u$.
Step 3Explain the method: The axes are not perpendicular, so $F\cos\theta$ does not give the components. Use the triangle formed by $F_u$, $F_v$ and $F$ and the law of sines.
Step 4Find the angle between F and the v-axis: $105^{\circ} - 40^{\circ} = 65^{\circ}$.
Step 5Redraw as a triangle: Place $F_u$ along $u$ from $O$, then $F_v$ (parallel to $v$) from the tip of $F_u$ to the tip of $F$. This is tip-to-tail addition $F_u + F_v = F$.
Step 6Find the angle opposite the v-component: The angle at $O$ between $F_u$ and $F$ is $40^{\circ}$; it faces side $F_v$.
Step 7Find the angle opposite the u-component: The angle at the tip of $F$, between $F$ and the side parallel to $v$, is $65^{\circ}$; it faces side $F_u$.
Step 8Find the angle opposite F: The angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$: $180^{\circ} - 40^{\circ} - 65^{\circ} = 75^{\circ}$.
Step 9Write the law of sines: $\dfrac{F_u}{\sin 65^{\circ}} = \dfrac{F}{\sin 75^{\circ}}$.
Step 10Rearrange: $F_u = F\,\dfrac{\sin 65^{\circ}}{\sin 75^{\circ}}$.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$F_u = (2.5\ \mathrm{kN})\frac{0.9063}{0.9659}$$
Step 12State the result: $F_u = 2.346\ \mathrm{kN} \approx 2.35\ \mathrm{kN}$, directed along the positive $u$-axis.
Step 13Check reasonableness: The same triangle gives $F_v = 2.5\sin 40^{\circ}/\sin 75^{\circ} = 1.66\ \mathrm{kN}$. Since $F$ lies closer to the $u$-axis than to the $v$-axis, the larger component should be along $u$, as found.
Worked Solution
Component triangle along u and v
Draw the parallelogram: From the tip of $F$ draw one line parallel to the $u$-axis and one parallel to the $v$-axis. They cut the axes at the tips of $F_u$ and $F_v$, forming a parallelogram with $F$ as its diagonal. List knowns and unknowns: $F = 2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$; angle from $u$ to $F$ is $40^{\circ}$; angle from $u$ to $v$ is $105^{\circ}$. Unknown: $F_u$. Explain the method: The axes are not perpendicular, so $F\cos\theta$ does not give the components. Use the triangle formed by $F_u$, $F_v$ and $F$ and the law of sines. Find the angle between F and the v-axis: $105^{\circ} - 40^{\circ} = 65^{\circ}$. Redraw as a triangle: Place $F_u$ along $u$ from $O$, then $F_v$ (parallel to $v$) from the tip of $F_u$ to the tip of $F$. This is tip-to-tail addition $F_u + F_v = F$. Find the angle opposite the v-component: The angle at $O$ between $F_u$ and $F$ is $40^{\circ}$; it faces side $F_v$. Find the angle opposite the u-component: The angle at the tip of $F$, between $F$ and the side parallel to $v$, is $65^{\circ}$; it faces side $F_u$. Find the angle opposite F: The angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$: $180^{\circ} - 40^{\circ} - 65^{\circ} = 75^{\circ}$. Write the law of sines: $\dfrac{F_u}{\sin 65^{\circ}} = \dfrac{F}{\sin 75^{\circ}}$. Rearrange: $F_u = F\,\dfrac{\sin 65^{\circ}}{\sin 75^{\circ}}$. Substitute numbers: $$F_u = (2.5\ \mathrm{kN})\frac{0.9063}{0.9659}$$ State the result: $F_u = 2.346\ \mathrm{kN} \approx 2.35\ \mathrm{kN}$, directed along the positive $u$-axis. Check reasonableness: The same triangle gives $F_v = 2.5\sin 40^{\circ}/\sin 75^{\circ} = 1.66\ \mathrm{kN}$. Since $F$ lies closer to the $u$-axis than to the $v$-axis, the larger component should be along $u$, as found.
Problem 19
Ch. 2 — Components from a Slope Triangle
A guy wire attached to a post at $A$ exerts a force $F = 650\ \mathrm{N}$ directed up and to the right along a line whose slope is given by a 5-12-13 triangle: 12 units horizontal, 5 units vertical. Determine the $y$-component of the force, $F_y$.
Guy-wire force with a 5-12-13 slope triangle
Determine $F_y$.
Solution
250 N
Free-body diagram
Force triangle similar to the slope triangle
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Place the tail of $F$ at $A$ and draw it up and to the right. Complete a right triangle with a horizontal leg $F_x$ and a vertical leg $F_y$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F = 650\ \mathrm{N}$; slope triangle 12 horizontal, 5 vertical, 13 hypotenuse. Unknown: $F_y$.
Step 3Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward.
Step 4Verify the slope triangle: $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$, so the hypotenuse is 13 units.
Step 5Recognize similar triangles: The force triangle ($F_x$, $F_y$, $F$) is similar to the slope triangle (12, 5, 13), so corresponding sides are in the same ratio. No angle is needed.
Step 6Write the ratio for the vertical side: $\dfrac{F_y}{F} = \dfrac{5}{13}$.
Step 7Rearrange: $F_y = \dfrac{5}{13}F$.
Step 8Substitute numbers: $$F_y = \frac{5}{13}(650\ \mathrm{N})$$
Step 9Compute: $F_y = 250\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 10Assign the sign and state the result: The force points upward, so $F_y = +250\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 11Check reasonableness: The horizontal component is $F_x = \tfrac{12}{13}(650) = 600\ \mathrm{N}$, and $\sqrt{600^2 + 250^2} = 650\ \mathrm{N}$ recovers the magnitude. The line is shallow, so $F_y < F_x$ as expected.
Worked Solution
Force triangle similar to the slope triangle
Draw the vector sketch: Place the tail of $F$ at $A$ and draw it up and to the right. Complete a right triangle with a horizontal leg $F_x$ and a vertical leg $F_y$. List knowns and unknowns: $F = 650\ \mathrm{N}$; slope triangle 12 horizontal, 5 vertical, 13 hypotenuse. Unknown: $F_y$. Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward. Verify the slope triangle: $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$, so the hypotenuse is 13 units. Recognize similar triangles: The force triangle ($F_x$, $F_y$, $F$) is similar to the slope triangle (12, 5, 13), so corresponding sides are in the same ratio. No angle is needed. Write the ratio for the vertical side: $\dfrac{F_y}{F} = \dfrac{5}{13}$. Rearrange: $F_y = \dfrac{5}{13}F$. Substitute numbers: $$F_y = \frac{5}{13}(650\ \mathrm{N})$$ Compute: $F_y = 250\ \mathrm{N}$. Assign the sign and state the result: The force points upward, so $F_y = +250\ \mathrm{N}$. Check reasonableness: The horizontal component is $F_x = \tfrac{12}{13}(650) = 600\ \mathrm{N}$, and $\sqrt{600^2 + 250^2} = 650\ \mathrm{N}$ recovers the magnitude. The line is shallow, so $F_y < F_x$ as expected.
Problem 20
Ch. 2 — Resultant of Three Coplanar Forces (Cartesian Vector Notation)
Three concurrent forces act on a bracket at $O$. $F_1 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ acts at $30^{\circ}$ above the positive $x$-axis. $F_2 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ acts up and to the left at $45^{\circ}$ above the negative $x$-axis. $F_3 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ acts down and to the right along a 3-4-5 slope (4 horizontal, 3 vertical). Determine the magnitude of the resultant force $F_R$.
Three concurrent forces on a bracket
Determine the magnitude $F_R$.
Solution
850 N
Free-body diagram
Component sums and the resultant
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Show the three forces at $O$ with their $x$ and $y$ components, then the resultant $F_R$ built from the summed components $F_{Rx}$ and $F_{Ry}$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above $+x$; $F_2 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ at $45^{\circ}$ above $-x$; $F_3 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ on a 3-4-5 slope, down and right. Unknown: $F_R$.
Step 3Set axes and state the plan: $+x$ right, $+y$ up. Step 1: resolve each force. Step 2: add the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components. Step 3: find the magnitude.
Step 4Resolve the first force: $\mathbf{F}_1 = \{800\cos 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} + 800\sin 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N} = \{692.8\,\mathbf{i} + 400.0\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 5Resolve the second force: It points left and up: $\mathbf{F}_2 = \{-600\cos 45^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} + 600\sin 45^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N} = \{-424.3\,\mathbf{i} + 424.3\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 6Resolve the third force: It points right and down: $\mathbf{F}_3 = \{\tfrac{4}{5}(500)\,\mathbf{i} - \tfrac{3}{5}(500)\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N} = \{400.0\,\mathbf{i} - 300.0\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 7Write the vector sum: $\mathbf{F}_R = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = F_{Rx}\,\mathbf{i} + F_{Ry}\,\mathbf{j}$.
Step 8Sum the x-components: $F_{Rx} = 692.8 - 424.3 + 400.0 = 668.6\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 9Sum the y-components: $F_{Ry} = 400.0 + 424.3 - 300.0 = 524.3\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 10Write the magnitude formula: $F_R = \sqrt{F_{Rx}^2 + F_{Ry}^2}$, from the Pythagorean theorem since $x$ and $y$ are perpendicular.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$F_R = \sqrt{(668.6)^2 + (524.3)^2} = \sqrt{721.8(10^{3})}\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 12State the result: $F_R = 849.6\ \mathrm{N} \approx 850\ \mathrm{N}$, directed at $\theta = \tan^{-1}(524.3/668.6) = 38.1^{\circ}$ above the positive $x$-axis.
Step 13Check reasonableness: Both resultant components are positive, so $F_R$ lies in the first quadrant, which matches a sketch in which the up-and-right pull of $F_1$ dominates.
Worked Solution
Component sums and the resultant
Draw the vector sketch: Show the three forces at $O$ with their $x$ and $y$ components, then the resultant $F_R$ built from the summed components $F_{Rx}$ and $F_{Ry}$. List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above $+x$; $F_2 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$ at $45^{\circ}$ above $-x$; $F_3 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ on a 3-4-5 slope, down and right. Write the magnitude formula: $F_R = \sqrt{F_{Rx}^2 + F_{Ry}^2}$, from the Pythagorean theorem since $x$ and $y$ are perpendicular. Substitute numbers: $$F_R = \sqrt{(668.6)^2 + (524.3)^2} = \sqrt{721.8(10^{3})}\ \mathrm{N}$$ State the result: $F_R = 849.6\ \mathrm{N} \approx 850\ \mathrm{N}$, directed at $\theta = \tan^{-1}(524.3/668.6) = 38.1^{\circ}$ above the positive $x$-axis. Problem 21
Ch. 2 — Unknown Force for a Resultant Along a Given Axis
Three cables pull on a ring at $O$. $F_2 = 5\ \mathrm{kN}$ acts along the positive $x$-axis. $F_3 = 3\ \mathrm{kN}$ acts down and to the right at $40^{\circ}$ below the positive $x$-axis. The third cable force $F$ acts up and to the left at $30^{\circ}$ from the positive $y$-axis. The magnitude of $F$ is adjusted so that the resultant of the three forces is directed along the positive $y$-axis. Determine the magnitude of this resultant $F_R$.
Three cable forces with a vertical resultant
Determine the magnitude of the resultant $F_R$.
Solution
10.7 kN
Free-body diagram
Components of the three forces and the vertical resultant
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Show $F$, $F_2$ and $F_3$ at $O$ with their components, and the required resultant $F_R$ pointing straight up along $+y$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F_2 = 5\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+x$; $F_3 = 3\ \mathrm{kN}$ at $40^{\circ}$ below $+x$; $F$ at $30^{\circ}$ from $+y$ toward $-x$, magnitude unknown. Condition: $F_R$ along $+y$. Unknowns: $F$, then $F_R$.
Step 3Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward.
Step 4Resolve the unknown force: Its angle is measured from the $y$-axis, so sine gives the $x$ part: $\mathbf{F} = \{-F\sin 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} + F\cos 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}$.
Step 5Resolve the second force: $\mathbf{F}_2 = \{5\,\mathbf{i} + 0\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 6Resolve the third force: $\mathbf{F}_3 = \{3\cos 40^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} - 3\sin 40^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN} = \{2.298\,\mathbf{i} - 1.928\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 7Translate the condition: A resultant along the $y$-axis has no $x$-component, so $F_{Rx} = 0$.
Step 8Write the x-sum: $F_{Rx} = -F\sin 30^{\circ} + 5 + 2.298 = 0$.
Step 9Solve for the unknown force: $F = \dfrac{5 + 2.298}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{7.298}{0.5} = 14.60\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 10Write the y-sum: $F_{Ry} = F\cos 30^{\circ} - 3\sin 40^{\circ}$.
Step 11Substitute numbers: $$F_{Ry} = (14.60)(0.8660) - 1.928 = 12.64 - 1.928 = 10.71\ \mathrm{kN}$$
Step 12State the result: Since $F_{Rx} = 0$, $F_R = F_{Ry} = 10.7\ \mathrm{kN}$, directed along the positive $y$-axis.
Step 13Check reasonableness: $F_{Ry}$ came out positive, so the resultant does point along $+y$ as required, and the leftward part of $F$, $14.60(0.5) = 7.30\ \mathrm{kN}$, exactly cancels the rightward pulls $5 + 2.298 = 7.30\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Worked Solution
Components of the three forces and the vertical resultant
Draw the vector sketch: Show $F$, $F_2$ and $F_3$ at $O$ with their components, and the required resultant $F_R$ pointing straight up along $+y$. List knowns and unknowns: $F_2 = 5\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+x$; $F_3 = 3\ \mathrm{kN}$ at $40^{\circ}$ below $+x$; $F$ at $30^{\circ}$ from $+y$ toward $-x$, magnitude unknown. Condition: $F_R$ along $+y$. Unknowns: $F$, then $F_R$. Set axes and sign convention: $+x$ to the right, $+y$ upward. Resolve the unknown force: Its angle is measured from the $y$-axis, so sine gives the $x$ part: $\mathbf{F} = \{-F\sin 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} + F\cos 30^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}$. Resolve the second force: $\mathbf{F}_2 = \{5\,\mathbf{i} + 0\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN}$. Resolve the third force: $\mathbf{F}_3 = \{3\cos 40^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} - 3\sin 40^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN} = \{2.298\,\mathbf{i} - 1.928\,\mathbf{j}\}\ \mathrm{kN}$. Translate the condition: A resultant along the $y$-axis has no $x$-component, so $F_{Rx} = 0$. Write the x-sum: $F_{Rx} = -F\sin 30^{\circ} + 5 + 2.298 = 0$. Solve for the unknown force: $F = \dfrac{5 + 2.298}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{7.298}{0.5} = 14.60\ \mathrm{kN}$. Write the y-sum: $F_{Ry} = F\cos 30^{\circ} - 3\sin 40^{\circ}$. Substitute numbers: $$F_{Ry} = (14.60)(0.8660) - 1.928 = 12.64 - 1.928 = 10.71\ \mathrm{kN}$$ State the result: Since $F_{Rx} = 0$, $F_R = F_{Ry} = 10.7\ \mathrm{kN}$, directed along the positive $y$-axis. Check reasonableness: $F_{Ry}$ came out positive, so the resultant does point along $+y$ as required, and the leftward part of $F$, $14.60(0.5) = 7.30\ \mathrm{kN}$, exactly cancels the rightward pulls $5 + 2.298 = 7.30\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Problem 22
Ch. 2 — Magnitude of a 3-D Cartesian Vector
The force acting on a hook at the origin $O$ is $\mathbf{F} = \{2.5\,\mathbf{i} - 4\,\mathbf{j} + 6\,\mathbf{k}\}\ \mathrm{kN}$. Determine the magnitude of the force.
Force vector and its component box
Determine the magnitude $F$.
Solution
7.63 kN
Free-body diagram
Box construction for the magnitude
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Draw a box with one corner at $O$ whose edges are the components: $2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+x$, $4\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $-y$ and $6\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+z$. The force $\mathbf{F}$ is the diagonal of the box, and $F'$ is its projection in the $x$-$y$ plane.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F_x = 2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$, $F_y = -4\ \mathrm{kN}$, $F_z = 6\ \mathrm{kN}$. Unknown: magnitude $F$.
Step 3State the coordinate system: A right-handed Cartesian system with unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$ along $x$, $y$, $z$.
Step 4Find the projection in the x-y plane: As for a 2-D vector, $F' = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$.
Step 5Combine the projection with the z-component: $F'$ and $F_z$ are perpendicular, so $F = \sqrt{(F')^2 + F_z^2}$.
Step 6Write the magnitude formula: $$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2}$$
Step 7Substitute numbers: $F = \sqrt{(2.5)^2 + (-4)^2 + (6)^2}\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 8Square each component: $(2.5)^2 = 6.25$, $(-4)^2 = 16$, $(6)^2 = 36$. The negative sign disappears on squaring.
Step 9Add: $6.25 + 16 + 36 = 58.25\ \mathrm{kN^2}$.
Step 10Take the square root: $F = \sqrt{58.25} = 7.632\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 11State the result: $F = 7.63\ \mathrm{kN}$.
Step 12Check reasonableness: The magnitude must exceed the largest component ($6\ \mathrm{kN}$) and be less than the sum of the component sizes ($12.5\ \mathrm{kN}$). The value $7.63\ \mathrm{kN}$ lies in that range.
Worked Solution
Box construction for the magnitude
Draw the vector sketch: Draw a box with one corner at $O$ whose edges are the components: $2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+x$, $4\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $-y$ and $6\ \mathrm{kN}$ along $+z$. The force $\mathbf{F}$ is the diagonal of the box, and $F'$ is its projection in the $x$-$y$ plane. List knowns and unknowns: $F_x = 2.5\ \mathrm{kN}$, $F_y = -4\ \mathrm{kN}$, $F_z = 6\ \mathrm{kN}$. Unknown: magnitude $F$. State the coordinate system: A right-handed Cartesian system with unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$ along $x$, $y$, $z$. Find the projection in the x-y plane: As for a 2-D vector, $F' = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$. Combine the projection with the z-component: $F'$ and $F_z$ are perpendicular, so $F = \sqrt{(F')^2 + F_z^2}$. Write the magnitude formula: $$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2}$$ Substitute numbers: $F = \sqrt{(2.5)^2 + (-4)^2 + (6)^2}\ \mathrm{kN}$. Square each component: $(2.5)^2 = 6.25$, $(-4)^2 = 16$, $(6)^2 = 36$. The negative sign disappears on squaring. Add: $6.25 + 16 + 36 = 58.25\ \mathrm{kN^2}$. Take the square root: $F = \sqrt{58.25} = 7.632\ \mathrm{kN}$. State the result: $F = 7.63\ \mathrm{kN}$. Check reasonableness: The magnitude must exceed the largest component ($6\ \mathrm{kN}$) and be less than the sum of the component sizes ($12.5\ \mathrm{kN}$). The value $7.63\ \mathrm{kN}$ lies in that range.
Problem 23
Ch. 2 — Coordinate Direction Angles
A force $F = 750\ \mathrm{N}$ acts on a bracket at $O$. Its coordinate direction angles with the positive $x$ and $y$ axes are $\alpha = 50^{\circ}$ and $\beta = 70^{\circ}$, and its $z$-component is known to be negative. Determine the coordinate direction angle $\gamma$ that the force makes with the positive $z$-axis.
Force with two known coordinate direction angles
Determine $\gamma$.
Solution
133 deg
Free-body diagram
Direction angles of F
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Show $\mathbf{F}$ from $O$ with the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ measured from the positive $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes to the vector. Because $F_z$ is negative, the vector dips below the $x$-$y$ plane.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F = 750\ \mathrm{N}$, $\alpha = 50^{\circ}$, $\beta = 70^{\circ}$, $F_z < 0$. Unknown: $\gamma$.
Step 3Recall the definition: The direction cosines are the components of the unit vector: $\mathbf{u}_F = \cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + \cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + \cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}$. Each angle lies between $0^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.
Step 4Write the governing relation: A unit vector has magnitude 1, so $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. The three angles are not independent.
Step 5Rearrange: $\cos^2\gamma = 1 - \cos^2\alpha - \cos^2\beta$.
Step 6Evaluate the known terms: $\cos^2 50^{\circ} = (0.6428)^2 = 0.4132$ and $\cos^2 70^{\circ} = (0.3420)^2 = 0.1170$.
Step 7Substitute numbers: $$\cos^2\gamma = 1 - 0.4132 - 0.1170 = 0.4698$$
Step 8Take the square root: $\cos\gamma = \pm\sqrt{0.4698} = \pm 0.6855$.
Step 9Choose the sign: $F_z = F\cos\gamma$ is negative, so $\cos\gamma = -0.6855$ and $\gamma$ must be greater than $90^{\circ}$.
Step 10Solve for the angle: $\gamma = \cos^{-1}(-0.6855) = 133.3^{\circ}$.
Step 11State the result: $\gamma = 133^{\circ}$. The rejected root, $46.7^{\circ}$, would give a positive $z$-component.
Step 12Check reasonableness: $\cos^2 50^{\circ} + \cos^2 70^{\circ} + \cos^2 133.3^{\circ} = 0.4132 + 0.1170 + 0.4698 = 1.000$, and $F_z = 750(-0.6855) = -514\ \mathrm{N}$ is negative as required.
Worked Solution
Direction angles of F
Draw the vector sketch: Show $\mathbf{F}$ from $O$ with the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ measured from the positive $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes to the vector. Because $F_z$ is negative, the vector dips below the $x$-$y$ plane. List knowns and unknowns: $F = 750\ \mathrm{N}$, $\alpha = 50^{\circ}$, $\beta = 70^{\circ}$, $F_z < 0$. Unknown: $\gamma$. State the result: $\gamma = 133^{\circ}$. The rejected root, $46.7^{\circ}$, would give a positive $z$-component. Check reasonableness: $\cos^2 50^{\circ} + \cos^2 70^{\circ} + \cos^2 133.3^{\circ} = 0.4132 + 0.1170 + 0.4698 = 1.000$, and $F_z = 750(-0.6855) = -514\ \mathrm{N}$ is negative as required.
Problem 24
Ch. 2 — Resultant of Two 3-D Forces
Two forces act on a screw eye at $O$. $F_1 = 300\ \mathrm{N}$ is inclined at $40^{\circ}$ above the $x$-$y$ plane, and its projection $F'$ onto the $x$-$y$ plane makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the positive $y$-axis, measured toward the positive $x$-axis. $F_2 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ has coordinate direction angles $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$, $\beta = 135^{\circ}$ and $\gamma = 60^{\circ}$. Determine the magnitude of the resultant force $F_R$.
Two forces on a screw eye in 3-D
Determine the magnitude $F_R$.
Solution
594 N
Free-body diagram
Cartesian components and the resultant
Step 1Draw the vector sketch: Show $\mathbf{F}_1$ with its projection $F'$ in the $x$-$y$ plane and its vertical leg $F_{1z}$, show $\mathbf{F}_2$ with its three direction angles, and show the resultant $\mathbf{F}_R$ as the diagonal of the parallelogram on $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$.
Step 2List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 300\ \mathrm{N}$ given by projection angles ($40^{\circ}$ above the $x$-$y$ plane, $30^{\circ}$ from $+y$ toward $+x$). $F_2 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ given by $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$, $\beta = 135^{\circ}$, $\gamma = 60^{\circ}$. Unknown: $F_R$.
Step 3State the plan: Write each force in Cartesian vector form, add like components, then take the magnitude.
Step 4Resolve the first force out of plane: $F_{1z} = 300\sin 40^{\circ} = 192.8\ \mathrm{N}$ (upward, positive).
Step 5Find the in-plane projection: $F' = 300\cos 40^{\circ} = 229.8\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 6Resolve the projection along x: The $30^{\circ}$ angle is measured from the $y$-axis, so $F_{1x} = F'\sin 30^{\circ} = 229.8(0.5) = 114.9\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 7Resolve the projection along y: $F_{1y} = F'\cos 30^{\circ} = 229.8(0.8660) = 199.0\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 8Write the first force in Cartesian form: $\mathbf{F}_1 = \{114.9\,\mathbf{i} + 199.0\,\mathbf{j} + 192.8\,\mathbf{k}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 9Verify the second force's angles: $\cos^2 60^{\circ} + \cos^2 135^{\circ} + \cos^2 60^{\circ} = 0.25 + 0.50 + 0.25 = 1$, so the three angles are consistent.
Step 10Write the second force in Cartesian form: $\mathbf{F}_2 = 500\{\cos 60^{\circ}\,\mathbf{i} + \cos 135^{\circ}\,\mathbf{j} + \cos 60^{\circ}\,\mathbf{k}\} = \{250.0\,\mathbf{i} - 353.6\,\mathbf{j} + 250.0\,\mathbf{k}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 11Add like components: $\mathbf{F}_R = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 = \{(114.9 + 250.0)\,\mathbf{i} + (199.0 - 353.6)\,\mathbf{j} + (192.8 + 250.0)\,\mathbf{k}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 12Simplify: $\mathbf{F}_R = \{364.9\,\mathbf{i} - 154.5\,\mathbf{j} + 442.8\,\mathbf{k}\}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 13Write the magnitude formula: $F_R = \sqrt{F_{Rx}^2 + F_{Ry}^2 + F_{Rz}^2}$.
Step 14Substitute numbers: $$F_R = \sqrt{(364.9)^2 + (-154.5)^2 + (442.8)^2} = \sqrt{353.1(10^{3})} = 594.3\ \mathrm{N}$$
Step 15State the result: $F_R = 594\ \mathrm{N}$.
Step 16Check reasonableness: The resultant is less than $F_1 + F_2 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$ and greater than $F_2 - F_1 = 200\ \mathrm{N}$, and both forces have upward parts, so a large positive $z$-component is expected.
Worked Solution
Cartesian components and the resultant
Draw the vector sketch: Show $\mathbf{F}_1$ with its projection $F'$ in the $x$-$y$ plane and its vertical leg $F_{1z}$, show $\mathbf{F}_2$ with its three direction angles, and show the resultant $\mathbf{F}_R$ as the diagonal of the parallelogram on $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$. List knowns and unknowns: $F_1 = 300\ \mathrm{N}$ given by projection angles ($40^{\circ}$ above the $x$-$y$ plane, $30^{\circ}$ from $+y$ toward $+x$). $F_2 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ given by $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$, $\beta = 135^{\circ}$, $\gamma = 60^{\circ}$.
